Liliane, welcome to Conversations. For people who don't know you yet, what do you make?
What I make are sound works from hospital wards. I've been recording how patients and caregivers talk about pain since 2015.
You started as a photographer, didn't you?
I did. By the time I left photography, I had worked with images for almost twenty years, and I needed a different medium.
So what was the breakthrough?
It was a nurse who changed everything. She asked me why nobody records the night shift, and that question is still the premise of my work.
Some critics say that sound work about illness is heavy-handed. Do they have a point?
Admittedly, some of it is. But the best pieces are restrained. They leave space for the listener.
We have one minute left. Would you work with a hospital outside Brazil?
If a hospital invited me, I would go, but only with consent from every patient. Let me wrap up there: listening is where the work begins.
What I make are sound works from hospital wards.

Five minutes feels short until you are the one speaking. The people who do it well have a plan, and they let the listener see it. They signpost: first I will tell you what I make, then how it started, and then where it is going. They pace themselves, so the first minute is not a race. And they are not afraid of silence. A pause is much better than a filler. Um, you know, like, sort of: every filler tells the audience that you are still searching. If you stumble over a word, do not apologize. Just say it again, slowly, and continue. Nobody remembers a stumble. People remember the one sentence you said clearly. And in the last thirty seconds, wrap up. Go back to the first idea, say it in a new way, and stop. Ending on time is a kind of respect.

Every few months I ask my students to record the same task again: five minutes about their own work. Then we listen to the first recording and the new one, side by side. That is the benchmark, and it is much more honest than a test. At B2, progress is rarely a single breakthrough. It is quieter than that. The sentences get longer. The pauses move: they stop happening in the middle of a phrase and start happening between ideas. The speaker holds back less, and builds on what was said a minute earlier instead of starting again. What I ask my students to notice is not how many mistakes they made, but which mistakes have disappeared. When you look back on two recordings, that is the real measure of a block of lessons.
